Dense and porous ceramics have been widely used for various biomedical applications. Current applications of bioceramics include bone grafts, spinal fusion, bone repairs, bone fillers, maxillofacial reconstruction, etc. Amongst the various calcium phosphate compositions, hydroxyapatite, which has a composition similar to human bone, has attracted wide interest. Much emphasis is given to tissue engineering, both in porous and dense ceramic forms. The current review focusses on the various applications of dense hydroxyapatite and other dense biomaterials on the aspects of transparency and the mechanical and electrical behavior. Prospective future applications, established along the aforesaid applications of hydroxyapatite, appear to be promising regarding bone bonding, advanced medical treatment methods, improvement of the mechanical strength of artificial bone grafts and better in vitro/in vivo methodologies to afford more particular outcomes. Keywords: biomaterials, dense ceramics, hydroxyapatite, bioceramics, properties 1. Introduction Surplus demands and requirements for synthetic bone substitutes have been experienced in the last few decades, owing to the number of accidents/trauma and inherent bone defects by birth/age/diseases. Significant demand from clinics is known in the fields of cranial, dental, maxillofacial, orthopedic and spinal applications. Recent improvements in materials and cell engineering and surgical bone grafting techniques have been a boon to cure many patients across the world. Constant innovation in stem cells, biomaterials, artificial organs and their recent success stories shows a clear evolution in the human biological sciences. Though the current technologies can be considered as mature, many developments and improvements are required to mimic the biological properties of a human closely. Submission received: 16 January 2023 / Revised: 22 February 2023 / Accepted: 5 March 2023 / Published: 7 March 2023 Abstract Hydroxyapatite (HA), the principal mineral of bone tissue, can be fabricated as an artificial calcium phosphate (CaP) ceramic and potentially used as bioceramic material for bone defect treatment. Nevertheless, the production method (including the applied sintering temperature) of synthetic hydroxyapatite directly affects its basic properties, such as its microstructure, mechanical parameters, bioabsorbability, and osteoconductivity, and in turn influences its biomedical potential as an implantable biomaterial. The wide application of HA in regenerative medicine makes it necessary to explain the validity of the selection of the sintering temperature. The main emphasis of this article is on the description and summarization of the key features of HA depending on the applied sintering temperature during the synthesis process. The review is mainly focused on the dependence between the HA sintering temperature and its microstructural features, mechanical properties, biodegradability/bioabsorbability, bioactivity, and biocompatibility. 1. Calcium Phosphate Bioceramics—Biomaterial Widely Used for Bone Tissue Regeneration Bone is a tissue with a high capacity for self-repair, allowing the reconstruction of a damaged fragment without involvement of scar tissue. Despite this fact, some clinical cases due to external factors or accompanying diseases require surgical intervention [1,2,3]. In orthopedic surgeries aiming to regenerate serious bone fracture or defects, autologous grafts are the first choice due to the highest probability of successful regeneration. Nevertheless, the harvesting of autologous tissue has some limitations: the small amount of healthy tissue that can be safely used for this purpose, the burden on the body and the cost of the potential additional surgery, and complications at the bone harvesting site [4,5,6,7]. The development of synthetic calcium phosphate (CaP) bioceramics emerges as a distinct strategy that can overcome the limitations related to autologous tissue collection [8]. In the scientific literature, the predominant types of CaPs used are: tricalcium phosphates (TCPs, Ca2(PO4)3), hydroxyapatite (HA, Ca10(OH)2(PO4)6), and biphasic calcium phosphates (BCPs) [9]. Some key differences observed between the listed CaP types determine the frequency of their use in the case of bone regeneration [10]. The optimal CaP-based biomaterial used in the regeneration of bone tissue should be characterized by biocompatibility, osteoconductivity (the ability to promote osteoblast adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation), and suitable mechanical parameters (compressive strength and Young’s modulus) close to the human bone. Additionally, the high porosity and high specific surface area (SSA) of HA are essential for its biodegradability (thus bioabsorbability in a living organism), high bioactivity (ability to form an apatite layer on the HA surface), and good osseointegration of the material with the host tissue [8,11,12]. Synthetic CaP bioceramics are obtained from chemical reagents by controlled synthetic processes that allows one to obtain the material with desired microstructural and physicochemical properties in order to fit the specific requirements of different clinical cases [9,13,14]. When the bone regeneration is impaired, the osteogenic potential of CaP-based grafts can be enhanced by combining them with drugs, growth factors, or cell-based therapies [15,16]. Although there is a large variety of CaP-based materials for bone regeneration on the market, including granules, powders, blocks, cements, scaffolds, etc. [15,17,18], CaP granules are still frequently used in orthopedics and maxillofacial surgeries to fill bone defects and stimulate the regeneration process [8]. The current article was prepared mainly according to the scientific contributions in the ScienceDirect and Web of Science databases using the keywords: hydroxyapatite; sintering; bioceramics; biocompatibility; cytotoxicity; bioactivity; biodegradation; microstructure; mechanical properties. The database search was double-checked and supported with Google Scholar. 2. Synthesis of Sintered Hydroxyapatite The functional and structural similarity of HA to a mineral composition that is present in teeth and bones explain its priority over other CaPs [19,20]. Historically, granules of dense hydroxyapatite (HA) obtained by sintering at high temperature (≥900 °C) were the first bioceramics used as synthetic bone grafts [8]. Particular interest in HA results from its high similarity to the mineral part of the bone matrix, its biocompatibility, and its ability to create a strong bond with bone tissue without the participation of fibrous tissue [21]. Traditionally, in order to obtain a material with a compact structure, hydroxyapatite powder is densified as a result of the action of one or a combination of the following factors: temperature, pressure, and time of exposure to high temperature [22]. Synthesis trends, parameter ranges, and practical implications

The literature indicates that hydroxyapatite processing is dominated by routes that combine powder synthesis, porosity generation, and densification stages. The most common processing routes reported in the evidence include dense HA synthesis by sintering, porous HA fabrication through pore-forming agents or foam-based methods, and advanced fabrication techniques such as freeze casting, gel-casting, and polymeric foam infiltration [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R4]. These methods are chosen because they allow control over porosity, pore size, and mechanical behavior while preserving HA’s bioactivity [N4-R2][N4-R5]. A review also notes that HA is often fabricated as granules, powders, blocks, cements, scaffolds, or other forms, with granules still frequently used in orthopedics and maxillofacial surgeries for bone defects [N5-F1].

A recurring temperature range in the literature is around 1200–1300 °C for sintering, with some studies reporting a promising sintering window at 1200–1300 °C that maximized densification, interfilament bonding, and defect elimination while suppressing unwanted effects [N2-R4]. Another review notes that HA is traditionally densified at high temperature (≥900 °C), which is why early dense HA granules were the first synthetic bone grafts used [N5-F1]. The evidence also suggests that sintering above 1300 °C can become problematic: one source reports that HA decomposes at around 1400 °C, forming TCP phase, while another shows that damage can occur above 1400 °C in pellets and that phase transformation behavior is strongly temperature-dependent [N1-R3][N2-F2]. These temperature thresholds are important because they mark the shift from densification to decomposition and phase change.

The practical implications are clear. Sintering at lower temperatures typically preserves more porosity and is used when high porosity is desired, whereas higher temperatures favor densification and mechanical strength but risk decomposition and loss of HA phase stability [N5-F1][N1-R3][N2-F2]. Heat treatment is also used in the literature as a post-sintering step to improve densification or reduce residual porosity, with one study explicitly mentioning heat treatments during plasma spraying of coatings and during sintering of porous blocks and granules [N6-R2]. This implies that heat treatment is not only a densification tool but also a way to manage defects, gas evolution, and phase stability [N2-R2][N6-R3].

Limitations and open questions remain. First, reproducibility is constrained by the strong dependence on temperature, powder preparation, and processing history, as the review notes that HA sintering temperature directly affects microstructure, mechanical properties, and biocompatibility [N5-F1]. Second, open questions include how to balance porosity and mechanical strength without sacrificing bioactivity, and how to maintain HA phase stability across a broader temperature window [N5-F1][N1-R3]. The evidence also points to unresolved issues around defect control, grain boundary quality, and intergranular bonding, especially when heat treatment is used to suppress decomposition or gas evolution [N2-R4][N6-R3]. In short, the field is mature enough to identify key trends, but the parameter space and defect behavior remain complex enough to justify ongoing research [N5-R1][N5-F1].

How sintering temperature affects porosity and microstructure

The evidence shows a clear temperature window: lower sintering temperatures favor higher porosity and less densification, whereas higher temperatures drive densification and reduce porosity, but may also trigger decomposition or phase transformation. A review states that HA is traditionally densified at high temperature (≥900 °C), and that sintering temperature directly affects microstructure, mechanical properties, and biocompatibility [N5-F1]. Another source reports that sintering temperature is a critical factor influencing phase stability, densification behavior, and sintered properties [N1-R1]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that densification dominates above a certain threshold, while porosity remains high below it [N5-F1][N1-R1].

Decomposition and phase transformation change HA composition and grain structure. The evidence shows that HA begins to decompose around 1400 °C, with the formation of TCP phase [N1-R3]. Another source reports that thermal decomposition of HAP gradually releases OH⁻ ions and transforms into OHAP between 1000–1360 °C, and above 1360 °C OHAP decomposes further [N6-R1]. A separate study notes that heat treatment at 1350 °C promotes coarsening and partial decomposition of HA into β-TCP [N6-R3]. These findings indicate that sintering or heat treatment above ~1300 °C can shift the material away from HA toward TCP or intermediate phases, altering both chemical composition and microstructure [N1-R3][N6-R1][N6-R3].

The relationship between sintering temperature and pore morphology and size is also established. The review emphasizes that sintering affects pore size, pore morphology, and the degree of porosity [N5-F1]. The phase-transformation study of HA foams found that foams transformed at lower temperatures than pellets due to higher surface area, and that sintering before phase transformation can create damage extending into the interior above 1400 °C in pellets [N2-F2]. This suggests that pore morphology and size are not only determined by the initial porosity generation method, but also by the temperature window through which the material is sintered [N2-F2]. In general, higher sintering temperatures tend to reduce porosity and refine grain structure, while lower temperatures preserve or increase porosity and may leave coarser, more irregular pores [N5-F1][N2-F2].

Overall, the evidence supports a clear tradeoff: sintering temperature controls whether the material is dense and strong or porous and less dense, and it also controls whether HA remains stable or decomposes into other phases [N5-F1][N1-R1][N6-R1]. The main takeaway is that the optimal temperature window depends on the desired balance between densification, porosity, phase stability, and microstructural refinement [N5-F1][N1-R1].

How heat treatment affects porosity and defect behavior

Heat treatment can reduce residual porosity or gas evolution, but it does so with a tradeoff between defect reduction and other microstructural changes. The evidence notes that heat treatments are used during sintering of porous blocks and granules, and during plasma spraying of coatings, implying that they are used to improve consolidation and reduce residual gas or porosity-related issues [N6-R2]. A phase-transformation study on HA foams found that sintering before phase transformation can create damage extending into the interior above 1400 °C in pellets, suggesting that uncontrolled residual gas evolution or phase change can leave defects behind [N2-F2]. Heat treatment may therefore help by allowing phase changes to occur under controlled conditions rather than leaving them as residual defects [N2-F2][N6-R2].

The effect of heat treatment on crystal defects, grain boundary quality, and intergranular bonding is positive in some cases but not universal. The phase-transformation study found that foams transformed at lower temperatures than pellets and that this did not create damage in the foam, while pellets developed damage above 1400 °C [N2-F2]. This implies that heat treatment can improve grain boundary and intergranular quality by reducing damage and allowing phase transitions to occur in a way that avoids microcracking or intergranular failure [N2-F2]. Another source reports that a sintering window of 1200–1300 °C maximized densification, interfilament bonding, and defect elimination while suppressing unwanted effects [N2-R4]. This directly supports the idea that heat treatment can improve grain boundary quality and bonding by eliminating defects and promoting densification [N2-R4].

Heat treatment can improve mechanical integrity when it suppresses defects and promotes densification, but it can compromise integrity when it induces decomposition or phase changes that degrade HA stability. The evidence shows that HA decomposes above 1360 °C and that heat treatment at 1350 °C promotes partial decomposition into β-TCP [N6-R1][N6-R3]. It also shows that phase transformation can create damage in pellets above 1400 °C [N2-F2]. In other words, heat treatment is beneficial when it enhances densification and defect elimination, but it becomes harmful when it drives decomposition, phase change, or damage formation [N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R3].

The practical implication is that heat treatment is a double-edged tool: it can reduce residual porosity and gas evolution, improve grain boundary quality and intergranular bonding, and enhance mechanical integrity when applied carefully; but it can also degrade HA composition and mechanical performance if the temperature window is not chosen appropriately [N6-R2][N2-F2][N6-R3].

How porosity and sintering affect mechanical properties

Porosity reduces compressive and flexural strength, and the evidence is direct on that point. A review reports that compressive strength and bending strength of dense HA ceramics fall in the range of 120–900 MPa and 38–250 MPa, respectively, and that the compressive strength of porous HA is strongly correlated with porosity volume [N3-F3]. Another source states that the compressive strength behavior of porous HA can be correlated exponentially with porosity volume, with a correlation factor greater than 0.96 [N7-R1]. A further study notes that not only total porosity but also pore size can influence compressive strength [N7-R5]. This is consistent with the general understanding that pores act as stress concentrators, reducing load-bearing capacity and strength [N3-F3][N7-R1][N7-R5].

Densification and pore size also affect toughness and load-bearing capacity. The evidence shows that densification increases mechanical strength and toughness, as one review states that sintering increases mechanical strength and toughness due to increased densification [N2-R2]. It also notes that densification can reduce porosity and improve strength, while the addition of collagen or collagen/HAp coatings reduced porosity and enhanced mechanical properties [N3-R4]. This implies that as porosity decreases and densification increases, the material becomes stiffer and more load-bearing, but the relationship is not linear and depends on pore size [N2-R2][N3-R4]. The compressive-strength studies also show that smaller micropore size increases strength in both bending and compression [N7-R2], reinforcing the idea that pore size matters as much as porosity level [N7-R2].

The tradeoff between porosity, mechanical strength, and biological performance is a key theme in the evidence. HA is valued for its high porosity, which is essential for biodegradability, bioactivity, and osseointegration [N5-F1]. At the same time, high porosity lowers mechanical strength [N3-F3][N7-R1]. The review explicitly states that the optimal HA-based biomaterial should have biocompatibility, osteoconductivity, and suitable mechanical parameters close to human bone, plus high porosity and high specific surface area for bioabsorbability and good osseointegration [N5-F1]. This tradeoff is why the field must balance porosity with strength: high porosity improves biological performance but compromises mechanical load-bearing capacity, while densification improves strength but may reduce bioactivity and porosity [N5-F1][N3-F3]. The evidence also suggests that other factors, such as pore size and defect control, further refine this tradeoff [N7-R2][N7-R5].

## Integrated final answer on how sintering temperature and heat treatment affect porosity and mechanical properties of hydroxyapatite

Hydroxyapatite (HA) is a key bioceramic material whose porosity and mechanical properties are strongly shaped by sintering temperature and heat treatment. The evidence across the branch reports shows a consistent picture: sintering temperature controls whether the material is dense and strong or porous and less dense, while heat treatment can refine microstructure, reduce defects, and improve densification, but can also induce decomposition or phase changes that degrade HA stability. Below is a synthesis organized into sections on porosity, microstructure, mechanical properties, and practical implications.

---

## 1) Sintering temperature: the main driver of porosity and microstructure

### Temperature window where densification dominates versus where porosity remains high
The evidence shows a clear temperature window: lower sintering temperatures favor higher porosity and less densification, whereas higher temperatures drive densification and reduce porosity. A review states that HA is traditionally densified at high temperature (≥900 °C), and that sintering temperature directly affects microstructure, mechanical properties, and biocompatibility [N5-F1]. Another source reports that sintering temperature is a critical factor influencing phase stability, densification behavior, and sintered properties [N1-R1]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that densification dominates above a certain threshold, while porosity remains high below it [N5-F1][N1-R1].

### How decomposition or phase transformation changes HA composition and grain structure
Decomposition and phase transformation change HA composition and grain structure. The evidence shows that HA begins to decompose around 1400 °C, with the formation of TCP phase [N1-R3]. Another source reports that thermal decomposition of HAP gradually releases OH⁻ ions and transforms into OHAP between 1000–1360 °C, and above 1360 °C OHAP decomposes further [N6-R1]. A separate study notes that heat treatment at 1350 °C promotes coarsening and partial decomposition of HA into β-TCP [N6-R3]. These findings indicate that sintering or heat treatment above ~1300 °C can shift the material away from HA toward TCP or intermediate phases, altering both chemical composition and microstructure [N1-R3][N6-R1][N6-R3].

### Relationship between sintering temperature and final pore morphology and size
The relationship between sintering temperature and final pore morphology and size is also established. The review emphasizes that sintering affects pore size, pore morphology, and the degree of porosity [N5-F1]. The phase-transformation study of HA foams found that foams transformed at lower temperatures than pellets due to higher surface area, and that sintering before phase transformation can create damage extending into the interior above 1400 °C in pellets [N2-F2]. In general, higher sintering temperatures tend to reduce porosity and refine grain structure, while lower temperatures preserve or increase porosity and may leave coarser, more irregular pores [N5-F1][N2-F2].

---

## 2) Heat treatment: a double-edged tool for porosity and defect behavior

### How post-sintering heat treatment reduces residual porosity or gas evolution
Heat treatment can reduce residual porosity or gas evolution. The evidence notes that heat treatments are used during sintering of porous blocks and granules, and during plasma spraying of coatings, implying that they are used to improve consolidation and reduce residual gas or porosity-related issues [N6-R2]. A phase-transformation study on HA foams found that sintering before phase transformation can create damage extending into the interior above 1400 °C in pellets, suggesting that uncontrolled residual gas evolution or phase change can leave defects behind [N2-F2]. Heat treatment may therefore help by allowing phase changes to occur under controlled conditions rather than leaving them as residual defects [N2-F2][N6-R2].

### Effect on crystal defects, grain boundary quality, and intergranular bonding
Heat treatment can improve grain boundary quality and intergranular bonding. The phase-transformation study found that foams transformed at lower temperatures than pellets and that this did not create damage in the foam, while pellets developed damage above 1400 °C [N2-F2]. This implies that heat treatment can improve grain boundary and intergranular quality by reducing damage and allowing phase transitions to occur in a way that avoids microcracking or intergranular failure [N2-F2]. Another source reports that a sintering window of 1200–1300 °C maximized densification, interfilament bonding, and defect elimination while suppressing unwanted effects [N2-R4]. This directly supports the idea that heat treatment can improve grain boundary quality and bonding by eliminating defects and promoting densification [N2-R4].

### When heat treatment improves versus compromises mechanical integrity
Heat treatment can improve mechanical integrity when it suppresses defects and promotes densification, but it can compromise integrity when it induces decomposition or phase changes that degrade HA stability. The evidence shows that HA decomposes above 1360 °C and that heat treatment at 1350 °C promotes partial decomposition into β-TCP [N6-R1][N6-R3]. In other words, heat treatment is beneficial when it enhances densification and defect elimination, but it becomes harmful when it drives decomposition, phase change, or damage formation [N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R3].

## 3) How porosity and sintering affect mechanical properties

### How porosity reduces compressive and flexural strength
Porosity reduces compressive and flexural strength, and the evidence is direct on that point. A review reports that compressive strength and bending strength of dense HA ceramics fall in the range of 120–900 MPa and 38–250 MPa, respectively, and that the compressive strength of porous HA is strongly correlated with porosity volume [N3-F3]. ### How densification and pore size affect toughness and load-bearing capacity

## 4) Synthesis trends, parameter ranges, and practical implications

### Common processing routes used in the literature
The literature indicates that hydroxyapatite processing is dominated by routes that combine powder synthesis, porosity generation, and densification stages. The most common processing routes reported in the evidence include dense HA synthesis by sintering, porous HA fabrication through pore-forming agents or foam-based methods, and advanced fabrication techniques such as freeze casting, gel-casting, and polymeric foam infiltration [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R4]. These methods are chosen because they allow control over porosity, pore size, and mechanical behavior while preserving HA’s bioactivity [N4-R2][N4-R5]. A review also notes that HA is often fabricated as granules, powders, blocks, cements, scaffolds, or other forms, with granules still frequently used in orthopedics and maxillofacial surgeries for bone defects [N5-F1].

### Reported sintering and heat-treatment temperature ranges for optimal performance
A recurring temperature range in the literature is around 1200–1300 °C for sintering, with some studies reporting a promising sintering window at 1200–1300 °C that maximized densification, interfilament bonding, and defect elimination while suppressing unwanted effects [N2-R4]. Another review notes that HA is traditionally densified at high temperature (≥900 °C), which is why early dense HA granules were the first synthetic bone grafts used [N5-F1]. The evidence also suggests that sintering above 1300 °C can become problematic: one source reports that HA decomposes at around 1400 °C, forming TCP phase, while another shows that damage can occur above 1400 °C in pellets and that phase transformation behavior is strongly temperature-dependent [N1-R3][N2-F2]. These temperature thresholds are important because they mark the shift from densification to decomposition and phase change [N5-F1][N1-R3][N2-F2].

### Limitations, reproducibility issues, and open questions
Limitations and open questions remain. First, reproducibility is constrained by the strong dependence on temperature, powder preparation, and processing history, as the review notes that HA sintering temperature directly affects microstructure, mechanical properties, and biocompatibility [N5-F1]. Second, open questions include how to balance porosity and mechanical strength without sacrificing bioactivity, and how to maintain HA phase stability across a broader temperature window [N5-F1][N1-R3]. The evidence also points to unresolved issues around defect control, grain boundary quality, and intergranular bonding, especially when heat treatment is used to suppress decomposition or gas evolution [N2-R4][N6-R3]. In short, the field is mature enough to identify key trends, but the parameter space and defect behavior remain complex enough to justify ongoing research [N5-R1][N5-F1].

---

## 5) Bottom line

Sintering temperature and heat treatment together define the porosity and mechanical properties of hydroxyapatite. Lower sintering temperatures preserve porosity and may leave coarser, more irregular pores, while higher temperatures drive densification and reduce porosity, but risk decomposition or phase change [N5-F1][N1-R1][N2-F2]. Heat treatment can improve densification, grain boundary quality, and intergranular bonding, but it can also induce decomposition, phase change, or damage if applied outside the safe temperature window [N2-R4][N6-R1][N6-R3]. Porosity reduces compressive and flexural strength, while densification and smaller pore size increase toughness and load-bearing capacity [N3-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2]. The key tradeoff is between mechanical strength and biological performance: higher porosity improves bioactivity and osseointegration, but lowers mechanical strength; densification improves strength, but may reduce porosity and bioactivity [N5-F1][N3-F3]. Overall, the optimal HA material depends on the intended application and the balance of these competing factors [N5-F1][N3-F3].

How sintering temperature affects porosity and microstructure

The evidence shows a clear temperature window: lower sintering temperatures favor higher porosity and less densification, whereas higher temperatures drive densification and reduce porosity, but may also trigger decomposition or phase transformation. A review states that HA is traditionally densified at high temperature (≥900 °C), and that sintering temperature directly affects microstructure, mechanical properties, and biocompatibility [N5-F1]. Another source reports that sintering temperature is a critical factor influencing phase stability, densification behavior, and sintered properties [N1-R1]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that densification dominates above a certain threshold, while porosity remains high below it [N5-F1][N1-R1].

Decomposition and phase transformation change HA composition and grain structure. The evidence shows that HA begins to decompose around 1400 °C, with the formation of TCP phase [N1-R3]. Another source reports that thermal decomposition of HAP gradually releases OH⁻ ions and transforms into OHAP between 1000–1360 °C, and above 1360 °C OHAP decomposes further [N6-R1]. A separate study notes that heat treatment at 1350 °C promotes coarsening and partial decomposition of HA into β-TCP [N6-R3]. These findings indicate that sintering or heat treatment above ~1300 °C can shift the material away from HA toward TCP or intermediate phases, altering both chemical composition and microstructure [N1-R3][N6-R1][N6-R3].

The relationship between sintering temperature and pore morphology and size is also established. The review emphasizes that sintering affects pore size, pore morphology, and the degree of porosity [N5-F1]. The phase-transformation study of HA foams found that foams transformed at lower temperatures than pellets due to higher surface area, and that sintering before phase transformation can create damage extending into the interior above 1400 °C in pellets [N2-F2]. This suggests that pore morphology and size are not only determined by the initial porosity generation method, but also by the temperature window through which the material is sintered [N2-F2]. In general, higher sintering temperatures tend to reduce porosity and refine grain structure, while lower temperatures preserve or increase porosity and may leave coarser, more irregular pores [N5-F1][N2-F2].

Overall, the evidence supports a clear tradeoff: sintering temperature controls whether the material is dense and strong or porous and less dense, and it also controls whether HA remains stable or decomposes into other phases [N5-F1][N1-R1][N6-R1]. The main takeaway is that the optimal temperature window depends on the desired balance between densification, porosity, phase stability, and microstructural refinement [N5-F1][N1-R1].

The phase-transformation study found that foams transformed at lower temperatures than pellets and that this did not create damage in the foam, while pellets developed damage above 1400 °C [N2-F2]. Porosity reduces compressive and flexural strength, and the evidence is direct on that point. A review reports that compressive strength and bending strength of dense HA ceramics fall in the range of 120–900 MPa and 38–250 MPa, respectively, and that the compressive strength of porous HA is strongly correlated with porosity volume [N3-F3]. This is consistent with the general understanding that pores act as stress concentrators, reducing load-bearing capacity and strength [N3-F3][N7-R1][N7-R5].

The evidence shows that densification increases mechanical strength and toughness, as one review states that sintering increases mechanical strength and toughness due to increased densification [N2-R2]. HA is valued for its high porosity, which is essential for biodegradability, bioactivity, and osseointegration [N5-F1]. At the same time, high porosity lowers mechanical strength [N3-F3][N7-R1]. The review explicitly states that the optimal HA-based biomaterial should have biocompatibility, osteoconductivity, and suitable mechanical parameters close to human bone, plus high porosity and high specific surface area for bioabsorbability and good osseointegration [N5-F1]. This tradeoff is why the field must balance porosity with strength: high porosity improves biological performance but compromises mechanical load-bearing capacity, while densification improves strength but may reduce bioactivity and porosity [N5-F1][N3-F3]. ## 1) Sintering temperature: the main driver of porosity and microstructure

## 2) Heat treatment: a double-edged tool for porosity and defect behavior

## 4) Synthesis trends, parameter ranges, and practical implications

Limitations and open questions remain. Sintering temperature and heat treatment together define the porosity and mechanical properties of hydroxyapatite. ## Integrated final answer on how sintering temperature and heat treatment affect porosity and mechanical properties of hydroxyapatite

Hydroxyapatite (HA) is a key bioceramic material whose porosity and mechanical properties are strongly shaped by sintering temperature and heat treatment. The evidence across the branch reports shows a consistent picture: sintering temperature controls whether the material is dense and strong or porous and less dense, while heat treatment can refine microstructure, reduce defects, and improve densification, but can also induce decomposition or phase changes that degrade HA stability. Below is a synthesis organized into sections on porosity, microstructure, mechanical properties, and practical implications.

---

## 1) Sintering temperature: the main driver of porosity and microstructure

### Temperature window where densification dominates versus where porosity remains high
The evidence shows a clear temperature window: lower sintering temperatures favor higher porosity and less densification, whereas higher temperatures drive densification and reduce porosity. A review states that HA is traditionally densified at high temperature (≥900 °C), and that sintering temperature directly affects microstructure, mechanical properties, and biocompatibility [N5-F1]. Another source reports that sintering temperature is a critical factor influencing phase stability, densification behavior, and sintered properties [N1-R1]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that densification dominates above a certain threshold, while porosity remains high below it [N5-F1][N1-R1].

### How decomposition or phase transformation changes HA composition and grain structure
Decomposition and phase transformation change HA composition and grain structure. The evidence shows that HA begins to decompose around 1400 °C, with the formation of TCP phase [N1-R3]. Another source reports that thermal decomposition of HAP gradually releases OH⁻ ions and transforms into OHAP between 1000–1360 °C, and above 1360 °C OHAP decomposes further [N6-R1]. A separate study notes that heat treatment at 1350 °C promotes coarsening and partial decomposition of HA into β-TCP [N6-R3]. These findings indicate that sintering or heat treatment above ~1300 °C can shift the material away from HA toward TCP or intermediate phases, altering both chemical composition and microstructure [N1-R3][N6-R1][N6-R3].

### Relationship between sintering temperature and final pore morphology and size
The relationship between sintering temperature and final pore morphology and size is also established. The review emphasizes that sintering affects pore size, pore morphology, and the degree of porosity [N5-F1]. The phase-transformation study of HA foams found that foams transformed at lower temperatures than pellets due to higher surface area, and that sintering before phase transformation can create damage extending into the interior above 1400 °C in pellets [N2-F2]. This suggests that pore morphology and size are not only determined by the initial porosity generation method, but also by the temperature window through which the material is sintered [N2-F2]. In general, higher sintering temperatures tend to reduce porosity and refine grain structure, while lower temperatures preserve or increase porosity and may leave coarser, more irregular pores [N5-F1][N2-F2].

---

## 2) Heat treatment: a double-edged tool for porosity and defect behavior

### How post-sintering heat treatment reduces residual porosity or gas evolution
Heat treatment can reduce residual porosity or gas evolution. The evidence notes that heat treatments are used during sintering of porous blocks and granules, and during plasma spraying of coatings, implying that they are used to improve consolidation and reduce residual gas or porosity-related issues [N6-R2]. A phase-transformation study on HA foams found that sintering before phase transformation can create damage extending into the interior above 1400 °C in pellets, suggesting that uncontrolled residual gas evolution or phase change can leave defects behind [N2-F2]. Heat treatment may therefore help by allowing phase changes to occur under controlled conditions rather than leaving them as residual defects [N2-F2][N6-R2].

### Effect on crystal defects, grain boundary quality, and intergranular bonding
Heat treatment can improve grain boundary quality and intergranular bonding. The phase-transformation study found that foams transformed at lower temperatures than pellets and that this did not create damage in the foam, while pellets developed damage above 1400 °C [N2-F2]. This implies that heat treatment can improve grain boundary and intergranular quality by reducing damage and allowing phase transitions to occur in a way that avoids microcracking or intergranular failure [N2-F2]. Another source reports that a sintering window of 1200–1300 °C maximized densification, interfilament bonding, and defect elimination while suppressing unwanted effects [N2-R4]. This directly supports the idea that heat treatment can improve grain boundary quality and bonding by eliminating defects and promoting densification [N2-R4].

### When heat treatment improves versus compromises mechanical integrity
Heat treatment can improve mechanical integrity when it suppresses defects and promotes densification, but it can compromise integrity when it induces decomposition or phase changes that degrade HA stability. The evidence shows that HA decomposes above 1360 °C and that heat treatment at 1350 °C promotes partial decomposition into β-TCP [N6-R1][N6-R3]. It also shows that phase transformation can create damage in pellets above 1400 °C [N2-F2]. In other words, heat treatment is beneficial when it enhances densification and defect elimination, but it becomes harmful when it drives decomposition, phase change, or damage formation [N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R3].

---

## 3) How porosity and sintering affect mechanical properties

### How porosity reduces compressive and flexural strength
Porosity reduces compressive and flexural strength, and the evidence is direct on that point. A review reports that compressive strength and bending strength of dense HA ceramics fall in the range of 120–900 MPa and 38–250 MPa, respectively, and that the compressive strength of porous HA is strongly correlated with porosity volume [N3-F3]. Another source states that the compressive strength behavior of porous HA can be correlated exponentially with porosity volume, with a correlation factor greater than 0.96 [N7-R1]. A further study notes that not only total porosity but also pore size can influence compressive strength [N7-R5]. This is consistent with the general understanding that pores act as stress concentrators, reducing load-bearing capacity and strength [N3-F3][N7-R1][N7-R5].

### How densification and pore size affect toughness and load-bearing capacity
Densification and pore size also affect toughness and load-bearing capacity. The evidence shows that densification increases mechanical strength and toughness, as one review states that sintering increases mechanical strength and toughness due to increased densification [N2-R2]. It also notes that densification can reduce porosity and improve strength, while the addition of collagen or collagen/HAp coatings reduced porosity and enhanced mechanical properties [N3-R4]. This implies that as porosity decreases and densification increases, the material becomes stiffer and more load-bearing, but the relationship is not linear and depends on pore size [N2-R2][N3-R4]. The compressive-strength studies also show that smaller micropore size increases strength in both bending and compression [N7-R2], reinforcing the idea that pore size matters as much as porosity level [N7-R2].

### Tradeoff between porosity, mechanical strength, and biological performance
The tradeoff between porosity, mechanical strength, and biological performance is a key theme in the evidence. HA is valued for its high porosity, which is essential for biodegradability, bioactivity, and osseointegration [N5-F1]. At the same time, high porosity lowers mechanical strength [N3-F3][N7-R1]. The review explicitly states that the optimal HA-based biomaterial should have biocompatibility, osteoconductivity, and suitable mechanical parameters close to human bone, plus high porosity and high specific surface area for bioabsorbability and good osseointegration [N5-F1]. This tradeoff is why the field must balance porosity with strength: high porosity improves biological performance but compromises mechanical load-bearing capacity, while densification improves strength but may reduce bioactivity and porosity [N5-F1][N3-F3]. The evidence also suggests that other factors, such as pore size and defect control, further refine this tradeoff [N7-R2][N7-R5].

---

## 4) Synthesis trends, parameter ranges, and practical implications

### Common processing routes used in the literature
The literature indicates that hydroxyapatite processing is dominated by routes that combine powder synthesis, porosity generation, and densification stages. The most common processing routes reported in the evidence include dense HA synthesis by sintering, porous HA fabrication through pore-forming agents or foam-based methods, and advanced fabrication techniques such as freeze casting, gel-casting, and polymeric foam infiltration [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R4]. These methods are chosen because they allow control over porosity, pore size, and mechanical behavior while preserving HA’s bioactivity [N4-R2][N4-R5]. A review also notes that HA is often fabricated as granules, powders, blocks, cements, scaffolds, or other forms, with granules still frequently used in orthopedics and maxillofacial surgeries for bone defects [N5-F1].

### Reported sintering and heat-treatment temperature ranges for optimal performance
A recurring temperature range in the literature is around 1200–1300 °C for sintering, with some studies reporting a promising sintering window at 1200–1300 °C that maximized densification, interfilament bonding, and defect elimination while suppressing unwanted effects [N2-R4]. Another review notes that HA is traditionally densified at high temperature (≥900 °C), which is why early dense HA granules were the first synthetic bone grafts used [N5-F1]. The evidence also suggests that sintering above 1300 °C can become problematic: one source reports that HA decomposes at around 1400 °C, forming TCP phase, while another shows that damage can occur above 1400 °C in pellets and that phase transformation behavior is strongly temperature-dependent [N1-R3][N2-F2]. These temperature thresholds are important because they mark the shift from densification to decomposition and phase change [N5-F1][N1-R3][N2-F2].

### Limitations, reproducibility issues, and open questions
Limitations and open questions remain. First, reproducibility is constrained by the strong dependence on temperature, powder preparation, and processing history, as the review notes that HA sintering temperature directly affects microstructure, mechanical properties, and biocompatibility [N5-F1]. Second, open questions include how to balance porosity and mechanical strength without sacrificing bioactivity, and how to maintain HA phase stability across a broader temperature window [N5-F1][N1-R3]. The evidence also points to unresolved issues around defect control, grain boundary quality, and intergranular bonding, especially when heat treatment is used to suppress decomposition or gas evolution [N2-R4][N6-R3]. In short, the field is mature enough to identify key trends, but the parameter space and defect behavior remain complex enough to justify ongoing research [N5-R1][N5-F1].

---

## 5) Bottom line

Sintering temperature and heat treatment together define the porosity and mechanical properties of hydroxyapatite. Lower sintering temperatures preserve porosity and may leave coarser, more irregular pores, while higher temperatures drive densification and reduce porosity, but risk decomposition or phase change [N5-F1][N1-R1][N2-F2]. Heat treatment can improve densification, grain boundary quality, and intergranular bonding, but it can also induce decomposition, phase change, or damage if applied outside the safe temperature window [N2-R4][N6-R1][N6-R3]. Porosity reduces compressive and flexural strength, while densification and smaller pore size increase toughness and load-bearing capacity [N3-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2]. The key tradeoff is between mechanical strength and biological performance: higher porosity improves bioactivity and osseointegration, but lowers mechanical strength; densification improves strength, but may reduce porosity and bioactivity [N5-F1][N3-F3]. Overall, the optimal HA material depends on the intended application and the balance of these competing factors [N5-F1][N3-F3].
